# Testing the generation of `Innovation`s

## Definition of epidemic parameters
In a population of fixed size, the \(\SIR\) epidemic runs under the following stochastic dynamics:
\begin{tabbing}
\emph{Xemovals:}\qquad\= \(S\to S-1\), \= \((R \to R+1\) \= occurs at rate \(\beta \, I\), \kill
\emph{Infections:}    \> \(S\to S-1\),   \> \(I \to I+1\) \> occurs at rate \(\alpha \, S \, I\),\\
\emph{Removals:}      \> \(I \to I-1\),  \> \(R \to R+1\) \> occurs at rate \(\beta \, I\).     
\end{tabbing}
The structural parameter of epidemic `duration` 
(a positive real number)
and the `initial1` configuration
(of `SIR` type) are given by
`julia` constants,
as are the per-pair infection rate `α` and the per-individual rate of removal `β`.
The population size is computed as part of the construction of `initial1`.
```{julia}
const duration = 2.0;
const α, β = 0.2, 1.5;
const initial1 = SIR(0.0, 5, 1, 0);
const n₁ = initial1.n ;
println("Total population size is $n₁.")

samplesize = 10000 ;
```

## Simulation and storage of results
A sample of a random `Innovation` (with no conditional removals),
based on \(n=n_1\) time lines,
is generated using the following invocation:
`generate_innovation(initial1.n, duration, α=α, β=β)`.
Total numbers of `Infection`s with specified `infectee` marks
and numbers of `Removal`s with specified `target` marks are tabulated.
The logic here is as follows:

(a) a given time line \(x\) accumulates infections arising from contacts between
a `target` time line (must lie strictly below time line \(x\))
and
an `infectee` time line (must be at time line \(x\) or higher)
thus occurring at a rate \((x-1)(n_1-x+1) α\);

(b) a given time line \(x\) accumulates removals arising from each of the time lines
\(x\) and lower,
thus removals for time line \(x\) must occur at a rate \(x β\).

The following function returns a `DataFrame` of time line identifiers, and
also counts
per time line of infections, removals
and differenced removals together with their expected numbers:

```{julia}
function simulate_innovations(n, t, α, β, samplesize)
  df = DataFrame() ;

  df[:, "Time line"]      = 1:n
  df.infections          .= 0 ;
  df[:, "𝔼[infections]"]  = [(x - 1) * (n - x + 1) *  α * samplesize * t for x in 1:n] ;
  df.removals            .= 0 ;
  df[:, "𝔼[removals]"]    = [β * x * samplesize * t for x in 1:n] ;
  
  for x in 1:samplesize
    iv = generate_innovation(n, t, α=α, β=β)
    df.infections += [length([z for z in iv.infections if z.infectee == i]) for i in 1:n]
    df.removals   += [length([z for z in iv.removals   if z.target   <= i]) for i in 1:n]
  end
  
  df[:, "Δremovals"]    = [df.removals[1];          diff(df.removals)]
  df[:, "𝔼[Δremovals]"] = [df[:, "𝔼[removals]"][1]; diff(df[:, "𝔼[removals]"])]
  
  return df
end ;
```
\newpage

```{julia}
data = simulate_innovations(n₁, duration, α, β, samplesize)
pretty_table(data)
```

The actual simulation computations, together with expected mean numbers, are as follows:
```{julia}
short_list = ["Time line", "infections", "𝔼[infections]", "removals", "𝔼[removals]"]
pretty_table(data[:, short_list]; header = short_list, alignment=[:l, :r, :r, :r, :r],
  formatters = ft_printf("%5d"))
```

## Statistical analysis
The `removals` column in `data` is cumulative, so independent data is obtained from `Δremovals`.
```{julia}
lagged_list = ["Time line", "infections", "𝔼[infections]", "Δremovals", "𝔼[Δremovals]"]
pretty_table(data[:, lagged_list]; header = lagged_list, alignment=[:l, :r, :r, :r, :r], 
  formatters = ft_printf("%6d"));
```
Entries in both of `infections` and `Δremovals` are independent Poisson
with mean given by the corresponding `𝔼[...]`. The 
normal approximation to the Poisson distribution applies here.
```{julia}
function display_simulation_results(df)
  data[:, "p-value (inf)"] = 
    2ccdf(Normal(), abs.(df.infections - df[:, "𝔼[infections]"]) ./ .√(df[:, "𝔼[infections]"]))
  data[:, "p-value (rem)"] = 
    2ccdf(Normal(), abs.(df.removals - df[:, "𝔼[removals]"]) ./ .√(df[:, "𝔼[removals]"]))
  long_list  = ["Time line", "infections", "𝔼[infections]", "p-value (inf)", "Δremovals", "𝔼[Δremovals]", "p-value (rem)"]
  long_list0 = ["Time line", "infections", "𝔼[infections]", "p-value", "Δremovals", "𝔼[Δremovals]", "p-value"]
  pretty_table(df[:, long_list], header=long_list0, alignment=[:l, :r, :r, :l, :r, :r, :l],
    formatters = ((v, i, j)->(isnan(v) ? "---" : (j > 3 && v<=0.05 ? "$(round(v, digits=2))**" : v)),
                  ft_printf("%5d", [3,6]), ft_printf("%1.2f", [4,7])))
end ;
```

```{julia}
println("Total population size is $n₁; simulation uses $samplesize replicates:")
display_simulation_results(data)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Assessment
In a sequence of \(11\) independent \(Z\)-tests, no \(p\)-values are at the \(0.01\) level or lower.
:::

## An example using a larger population.
This repeats the simulations of the previous section for a larger population.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
const initial2 = SIR(0.0, 10, 1, 0)
const n₂ = initial2.n ;

println("Total population size is $n₂; simulation uses $samplesize replicates:")
data = simulate_innovations(n₂, duration, α, β, samplesize) 

pretty_table(data[:, lagged_list], header = lagged_list, alignment=[:l, :r, :r, :r, :r], 
  formatters = ft_printf("%6d"));
display_simulation_results(data)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Assessment
In a sequence of \(21\) independent \(Z\)-tests there is just one \(p\)-value at the \(0.01\) level or lower.
:::

## An example using a still larger population.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
const initial3 = SIR(0.0, 15, 1, 0)
const n₃ = initial3.n ;

println("Total population size is $n₃; simulation uses $samplesize replicates:")
data = simulate_innovations(n₃, duration, α, β, samplesize) 

display_simulation_results(data)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Assessment
In a sequence of \(31\) independent \(Z\)-tests there are no \(p\)-values at the \(0.01\) level or lower.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Overall assessment
In a total of \(63\) independent \(Z\)-tests, only one of the \(p\)-values sinks to the level of \(0.01\).
:::
